newsitem.title: CHINA: HK labour movement blasts union rights laws curbs.
newsitem.headline: HK labour movement blasts union rights laws curbs.

text.p: Pro-democracy trade unions in Hong Kong on Saturday criticised a labour policy panel's decision to scrap a set of labour rights laws recently suspended by the territory's China-backed assembly.

The Labour Advisory Board, which advises the government on labour issues, on Friday recommended scrapping two laws, one on collective bargaining and the other banning discrimination against union members by employers.
Another law on the use of trade union funds would be amended after the board, which groups business, unions and government, reached a decision.
It is widely believed the government will adopt the proposal by the Labour Advisory Board.
The three laws were passed by an elected legislature one week before China regained control of Hong Kong from Britain on July 1.
Later that month, the Beijing-installed Provisional Legislature endorsed government bills freezing the three laws until October on the grounds that they might hurt Hong Kong's competitiveness.
"It seems they (the government and businesses) have all the power to do whatever they want now," trade unionist and ousted legislator Leung Yiu-chung said by telephone.
Leung was thrown out of office on July 1 when the Provisional Legislature replaced the elected chamber, along with other pro-democracy lawmakers.
"We will mobilise unions and workers to oppose the abolition of the labour laws," Leung said.
He said fellow trade unionist Lee Cheuk-yan was considering a legal challenge against the provisional legislature for exceeding its jurisdiction.

China set up the interim assembly to roll back democratic reforms spearheaded by former governor Chris Patten in the twilight of British rule, and said the provisional chamber would only pass laws that are necessary to the operation of the post-colonial administration.
The international labour movement has already expressed outrage over the China-backed government's move and bombarded the territory's leader Tung Chee-hwa with letters of protest.
The development was the latest in a series of moves to cut back democracy and civil liberties in the territory of 6.4 million people.
